key_insight: This study audits the mental health interventions 41 language models recommend when the same clinical case is presented by a clinician, caregiver, or patient. The provided abstract describes the audit design but does not report findings about how recommendations differ.
problem_solved: Addresses the need to evaluate what mental health interventions language models recommend and whether recommendations change depending on who asks, even when the underlying clinical information stays the same.
method: Presented 19 clinical case vignettes from three perspectives—clinician, caregiver, and patient—across five questions.
Collected 35,055 free-text responses from 41 language models and extracted every named intervention using a validated judge.
Asked 29 models to rate the full list of intervention options.
impact: The audit offers a framework for testing role-sensitive behavior in mental health AI. Practitioners can use this approach to investigate recommendation consistency and potential safety concerns before deployment.
visual_elements: Three user icons—clinician, caregiver, and patient—connected to the same clinical case.
Audit pipeline: case vignettes → model responses → intervention extraction → option ratings.
Scale callouts: 41 models, 19 vignettes, five questions, and 35,055 responses.
A labeled comparison-matrix schematic showing how intervention recommendations could be compared across user perspectives.
paper_title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
paper_authors: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah
